Neonatal Oceanic whitetip sharks emerge from their mothers at a total length of approximately 62.5 cm [Lb = approximately 62.5 cm], a value that aligns well with the lower range of reported size at birth for large-bodied carcharhinids. This initial length, documented from field observations of newborn individuals, reflects the substantial maternal investment characteristic of this viviparous species. Following parturition, the young pups exhibit rapid early growth, likely driven by the warm and productive pelagic waters they inhabit. Comparative data from closely related species suggest that this birth size provides a strategic advantage against early predation, as larger neonates are less vulnerable to mid-sized piscivorous fishes. The first weeks of independent life are critical, with the developing juveniles focusing on foraging efficiency to build somatic mass. This period of accelerated growth continues until the individuals approach a more stable phase of development, where energy is increasingly directed toward structural consolidation ahead of the lengthy journey to adulthood.

As these young sharks mature, a pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate size becomes evident. Females are the larger sex, attaining a maximum recorded total length of 400 cm [Li = 400 cm], which is notably greater than the 390 cm [Li = 390 cm] observed for males. This difference in ultimate length is a common pattern among elasmobranchs and is often linked to the considerable physical demands of gestation, as larger females can accommodate more or larger developing embryos. The attainment of this final size is a slow process, with growth rates decelerating significantly after the onset of reproductive activity. Individuals can take many years to reach these impressive dimensions, a timeline that underscores the species' relatively slow life history. The very largest adult females, approaching the 400 cm mark, are exceptionally rare in fishery catches, suggesting that only a small fraction of the population survives long enough to realize their full growth potential.

The onset of sexual maturity in the Oceanic whitetip shark occurs at markedly different total lengths between the sexes, reflecting their divergent life-history strategies. Females first become capable of reproduction upon reaching a total length of approximately 190 cm [Lp = approximately 190 cm], though this value can range from 180 to 200 cm based on regional variability. Males, in contrast, mature at a slightly smaller size, with puberty typically recorded at 180 cm [Lp = 180 cm] total length. This size-based maturation threshold is critical for population dynamics, as it determines the age at which individuals can first contribute to the next generation. Attaining these lengths requires several years of sustained growth in the open ocean, where food availability and water temperature play modulating roles. Once these pubertal lengths are crossed, the reproductive organs undergo full development, preparing the shark for a lifetime of breeding activity. The difference of 10 cm between the maturation lengths of males and females is a consistent feature across the species' range.

Reproductive output in this species is relatively modest but consistent. Under optimal thermal conditions, specifically at stable water temperatures of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], females produce between 1 and 15 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 1 and 15 pups per litter] in a single annual litter [F_R_i = single annual litter]. This annual fecundity is influenced by the female's body size and condition, with larger, more experienced mothers typically producing the largest litters. The gestation period, thought to last around a year, results in the birth of fully formed, free-swimming pups that receive no further parental care. This reproductive strategy, characterized by low fecundity and high per-offspring investment, renders the Oceanic whitetip shark particularly vulnerable to overfishing. The upper limit of 15 pups in a single year is only attained by the most robust individuals, while first-time mothers often produce smaller litters of just one or two pups. This constrained reproductive capacity is a key factor in the species' slow population recovery rates.

The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult is an estimated 167,400 grams [Wwi = 167,400 grams], marking the culmination of decades of somatic growth. This massive body mass, concentrated in the muscular torso and large pectoral fins, supports the shark's pelagic cruising lifestyle. Accompanying this impressive size is a considerable lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years] in the wild when living at a mean water temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C]. This longevity, combined with the late age at maturity and low reproductive rate, typifies a K-selected life history. Such a strategy is evolutionarily successful in stable, predictable environments, but it is highly susceptible to chronic mortality from human activities. The combination of reaching an asymptotic mass of 167,400 grams after many years of growth only to face a relatively long but vulnerable adult life highlights the conservation challenges facing this top pelagic predator.
